title: What is truth? (John 18:28–38)
hook: Pilate asks and doesn't wait for an answer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter at the charcoal fire, saying I am not. Your line was warming himself. Where did you step out of the crowd? Day six hundred forty-four.

In a museum in Manchester, England, there's a scrap of papyrus smaller than a credit card. It has a few lines of Greek on each side, and it's one of the oldest pieces of the New Testament anyone has ever found. Scholars usually date it to the second century. Of all the pages that could have survived from those early years, this one holds a few verses from today's passage. Jesus standing before Pilate. And on the back, part of the question Pilate asks. It's as if the oldest surviving page had been saving this scene.
screen: `ONE OF THE OLDEST NEW TESTAMENT PIECES.`

segments.voice: It's early morning. Jesus is brought to the Roman governor's headquarters. Pilate, the governor of Judea, is the one man in Jerusalem with the power to order a crucifixion, and the conversation shuttles back and forth between him and the prisoner. Pilate asks: are you a king? And Jesus answers, in the King James Bible, "My kingdom is not of this world." Then he says what he came for: "To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth. Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice." And Pilate says three words: "What is truth?" And then, John tells us, he went out again. He asks the biggest question in the room and walks away before anyone can answer. Four hundred years ago the English writer Francis Bacon opened an essay with this scene: "What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer." Was he jesting? Nobody knows his tone. Readers have heard it as sneering, as weary, as a politician who's heard too many sincere men. The Greek word for truth is aletheia, and in John it's more than correct information. Jesus has already said, I am the way, the truth, and the life. So in John's telling, Pilate asks what truth is while Truth is standing in front of him. The irony is the point. One more thing worth saying: Pilate then tells the crowd, I find in him no fault at all. Let's look back. This week: courage in trouble, the hour, keep them, be one, the garden, the fire, and now a question left hanging.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.`
`BORN TO BEAR WITNESS TO THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait for an answer today. Settle, and breathe. Think of a question you've been asking without really waiting for the answer. How are you doing, said in passing. What do you think, said while already reaching for your phone. Maybe a question you ask God, or yourself, and then change the subject. Pick one. For these minutes, ask it again, slowly, and then don't move on. Just wait. If you pray, you can ask it in prayer and leave a silence afterward. The bell holds the time.
What is truth? Pilate's question, asked of the man who said he came to bear witness to the truth, and left without waiting for the answer.
Your line: what is truth? Today, ask someone one real question, and then stay for the answer, all of it. Day six hundred forty-four, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians read Jesus's trial before Pilate during Holy Week, and many churches name Pilate every Sunday in the Creed: suffered under Pontius Pilate.

original.note: Greek: what is truth? aletheia, truth; in John, more than correct facts: something you can be 'of'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pilate asks a philosophy question.
what it means: the most powerful man in the room asks what truth is, and walks out before the answer.

what a scholar hears: the irony John sets up ('I am the truth', 14:6), and P52, a tiny papyrus in Manchester with verses from 18:31–33 and 18:37–38, often called the oldest known New Testament fragment.

notes: P52 (Rylands Greek Papyrus 457): contains John 18:31–33 (front) and 18:37–38 (back), commonly dated c. 125–175 though some scholars argue later. Confirm 'usually date it to the second century' and 'part of the question Pilate asks' (the back includes part of 18:38).
Bacon, 'Of Truth' (Essays, 1625) opening sentence: quoted from memory as the well-known wording; please verify against the 1625 text (early spelling may differ).
18:28 (the leaders not entering the praetorium to stay ritually pure for Passover) is left out to keep the day on one idea; consider whether it should be described.
